messages.subject: lavaan 0.5-19 released on CRAN
messages.subject_clean: lavaan 0.5-19 released on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Dear lavaan users,

I am happy to announce that lavaan 0.5-19 has been released on CRAN.

This version finalizes the changes (regarding the way general linear
equality constraints are handled) as described in this document. Please,
read it again: http://lavaan.ugent.be/notes/lavaan_eq_constraints.pdf

Other user-visible changes:

- the parameter estimates section of the summary() output has been
redesigned: it now repeats the section headers ('Est' 'Std.Err' etc),
and the number of digits after the decimal point can be changed, as in
summary(fit, nd = 5)

- the modindices() function now only shows modification indices for
'new' parameters (that are currently fixed to zero in the current
model); it does not give you information about what may happen if you
release (general) equality constraints; for that, we need the
lavTestScore() function

- new function lavTestScore() gives univariate/multivariate score tests
(aka Lagrange Multiplier tests) for releasing (typically equality)
constraints in the model

- lavPredict() now consistently ignores the structural component (ie all
regressions); its main purpose is to compute the values for latent
variables; if used with the type = "ov" argument, it will attempt to
compute the values of the indicators of these latent variables; if all
variables in a model are observed, it simply returns the observed
variables; in other words, despite its name, this function does not
'predict' new values for dependent variables, given values of
independent variables, as is common in regression models

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: running CFA in lavaan - displaying correlation between latent variables
messages.body_plain:
> 1. in this default setting, the correlation between the latent factors is calculated. is that true ?

The covariance is estimated by default.  To see the correlation, you can print the standardized solution, or you can choose to fix the latent variances to 1 using the argument "std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE"

> F1 ~ F2 adds the regression but i'm not sure i understand the difference and when should i add this

A (simple) regression slope is the covariance divided by the variance of the predictor.  They are therefore equivalent information and yield the same model fit, but they represent different theories.  Use a regression to represent the hypothesis that F2 directly affects F1 (and use the sem() function instead of the cfa() function). Use a covariance when you are agnostic about why F1 and F2 are related.

>  2. is there a way to plot the CFA to show the results but also include the correlation between the factors? i've looked into semPaths in the semPlot package but i don't understand what is displayed on the arrow connecting the latent factors. i think that it might be the covariance  but i'm not sure.

Go to the help page and look at the "what" argument.  what = "std" provides the correlation

> 3. lastly, how do i know to modify my model ( adding F1~~F2, fixing parameters, etc')?

If you are asking how to specify parameters in lavaan syntax, it sounds like you already know.  If you are asking why you would free parameters, that would be up to you.

SEMNET is a good resource for more general questions about SEM: http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

Terry

>    lavaan WARNING: modification indices do not reflect (yet) what

This is 0.5-18 specific, and it means that the MI values (below) simply
ignore the fact that they were constrained to be equal.

> However, the output shows:
>
> ANT =~ m1_nri15     10.471 for Group 1 and
> ANT =~ m1_nri15     18.108 for Group 2

There is nothing 'wrong' with these values. As all the other MIs, they
give the score test for what will happen if you release (only) this
parameter, one at a time.

> 2. Question: The mi-values should be equal (or not?).

For simple equality constraints, that would indeed make sense (and we
did this in <0.5-18). For more general equality constraints (think: a =
2b + c), things get more complicated. That is why we have included the
lavTestScore() function in 0.5-19.

 From 0.5-19 onwards:

- modindices() will only show MIs for 'new' parameters that were not
included as free parameters in the original model

- lavTestScore() gives 'MI' values (univariate and multivariate) for
what happens if you release (one or more) equality constraints

Yves.

1. "std.lv <http://std.lv>" changes the way the common factors are scaled in the solution.  It does not change the scaling of the observed variables.  The standardized solution (obtained by, for example, the function standardizedSolution(object), where object is your output object from running the cfa, sem or lavaan functions) only rescales parameter estimates and standard errors after the fact--it does not alter the parameter estimation process in any way.  It is purely cosmetic.

2.  EFA and CFA models tend to have many kinds of differences.  EFA models often have a variety of parameteres with nonzero values which are constrained to exactly 0 in a CFA, so results differ.  But all you can do is try it.  My guess if that the CFA will indicate that the soluti0on will be better if the two groups of items are allowed to load on separate factors, unless sample size is low or the correlation between factors is very close to 1.

3.  My impression has always been that lavaan syntax is remarkably straightforward and concise, and the variety of functions provided, including cfa() and sem() offer sensible defaults that make the job even easier.  Start with cfa(), enjoy the defaults, and go from there.
--Ed Rigdon

Background

I have 50 dichotomously scored test items (1=correct response, 0 = otherwise) and various items are presumed to load onto different dimensions. My research objective is to test the hypothesized multidimensional structure of the test against a simple baseline model assuming all items load onto a single dimension.

The multidimensional model I want to estimate is a second order model where items load onto the first order factors and then those first order factors load onto a common factor. The second order factors would all share a pairwise correlation.

R Code

The code I am using is below. I want the polychoric correlations; hence the use of the ordered() function. Additionally, I want to identify the model by fixing the variance of the latent variables to 1, which I believe is accomplished via the 'std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE' argument. >
> This version finalizes the changes (regarding the way general linear equality constraints are handled) as described in this document. Please, read it again: http://lavaan.ugent.be/notes/lavaan_eq_constraints.pdf
>
> Other user-visible changes:
>
> - the parameter estimates section of the summary() output has been redesigned: it now repeats the section headers ('Est' 'Std.Err' etc), and the number of digits after the decimal point can be changed, as in summary(fit, nd = 5)
>
> - the modindices() function now only shows modification indices for 'new' parameters (that are currently fixed to zero in the current model); it does not give you information about what may happen if you release (general) equality constraints; for that, we need the lavTestScore() function
>
> - new function lavTestScore() gives univariate/multivariate score tests (aka Lagrange Multiplier tests) for releasing (typically equality) constraints in the model
>
> - lavPredict() now consistently ignores the structural component (ie all regressions); its main purpose is to compute the values for latent variables; if used with the type = "ov" argument, it will attempt to
> compute the values of the indicators of these latent variables; if all variables in a model are observed, it simply returns the observed variables; in other words, despite its name, this function does not 'predict' new values for dependent variables, given values of independent variables, as is common in regression models

Hi, Yves

I tried to check measurement invariance for a model that included one latent variable defined by three continuous indicators and three latent variables, each defined by three categorical indicators. I revealed that by default Lavaan estimated a configural model with all thresholds fixed to be equal across groups.

However, if I understand the concept of MI correctly, the configural model should have group- specific estimates for each parameter, exluding only parameters restricted to achieve identification. > I do get a positive coefficient relating ants_bin to Bloom_bin, but as soon as I add additional factors to the regression, it becomes negative. Any idea why this could be happening or what it means?

This can happen.  A little Googling on "suppressor variables" and "partial mediation" should lead you to the kind of information you are looking for.  Consider signing up on SEMNET and searching their email archives -- several SEM experts regularly contribute there, and you will be able to find record of emails about the same issue you are curious about.

> Also, I am worried about the summary for the entire model, where the test statistics seem very low. I can make the model above a bit simpler by removing non-significant factors and get a few degrees of freedom back, but it doesn't seem to help much. Should I be worried about this?

I'm not sure what you mean by too low.  A high chi-squared (with low p value) is evidence against the null hypothesis that you model is a perfect description of the real data-generating process in nature.  Yes, more degrees of freedom yield a more powerful test of a more restricting hypothesis.  Trimming  non-significant paths is pretty common in path analysis, but I would recommend you start by conceiving of a more restricted model that you think could account for the data you observe, which you think is theoretically supportable.  Then test that model.

Terry

Well, seeing your data cleared up a few things -- that's why it is so important to provide information to reproduce the problem.   You do NOT have all continuous variables.  Some are binary, and a few of the ordered variables have fewer than 5 categories, which is the situation when you should really treat them as ordinal data:

http://psycnet.apa.org/psycinfo/2012-18631-001/

In addition to the warning about being unable to compute standard errors, lavaan issues a warning telling you that there was a negative residual variance, and to inspect the theta matrix.  Doing so would have shown you that the residual variance for insecurity3 was negative, which is often a good clue about the source of identification, (mis)specification, or estimation troubles.  The standardized solution helps reveal which indicators do not seem to "go with the rest" of the indicators for it's factor.  The indicators of insecurity, demand, emodemand, and ethical have either very low or altogether inconsistent intercorrelations (using Kendall's tau instead of Pearson correlation, since they are not continuous, or are very non-normal even when approximately continuous), so you need to question whether they really measure the same thing.  You provided N = 2000 data points, so I don't think sampling error is much of an issue here, and your sample size is large enough to have no fear of using the more appropriate DWLS estimator and declaring at least the binary variables as categorical (which DOES converge and provide standard errors).

You can see how I found this information in the attached R script, which includes some helpful basic data screening syntax.  In it, I calculated alc1 and smk1 by dividing by an arbitrary number to reduce their variances, but it probably isn't the same thing you did (which I didn't see evidence of in your previous posts).

messages.body_plain:
Mark,
I am not sure how EQS interprets the minus sign.  If you want to constrain the loading to be negative rather than just nudge Lavaan in that direction, you could use a method described by David Rindskopf (1984).  G1 and G2 are phantom variables.  The "loading" parameter is your constrained factor loading.  As a caution, I was not able to get this to converge without providing positive start values for the "a" parameter although the start values did not have to be close to the correct values.

# Begin code
require(lavaan)
sessionInfo()

simMod <- '
F =~ 1*i1 + 1*i2 + 1*i3 + 1*i4 + -1*i5
F ~~ 1 * F
i1 ~~ .5 * i1
i2 ~~ .5 * i2
i3 ~~ .5 * i3
i4 ~~ .5 * i4
i5 ~~ .5 * i5
'

simData <- simulateData(simMod)
round(cov(simData),2)

fitMod <- '
F =~ i1 + i2 + i3 + i4
G1 =~ 0
G2 =~ 0
i5 ~ -1*G2
G2 ~ label("a")*G1 + start(.5)*G1
G1 ~ label("a")*F + start(.5)*F
F~~1*F
G1~~0*G1
G2~~0*G2
i1~~i1
i2~~i2
i3~~i3
i4~~i4
i5~~ i5
loading := a*a*-1
'

lavParTable(fitMod)

fit <- lavaan(fitMod, simData)
summary(fit)
# End code

Keith

Rindskopf, D. (1984). Using phantom and imaginary latent variables to parameterize constraints in linear structural models.Psychometrika, 49, 37-47.

----------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY

messages.subject: Re: No. of indicators in factor for CFA
messages.subject_clean: No. of indicators in factor for CFA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You can have one, and by default that fixes the error variance to zero essentially making the latent variable and the indicator equal. You can of course fix the error to a non-zero value yourself, but I would not call that a factor analysis. It would be more like an errors-in-variables model.

A factor model requires at least two indicators, but two indicator models use the factor correlations for identification. This can result in very unstable loadings unless the factor correlations are high.

In practice, the minimum number is three, but four is better because it makes the each factor individually over identified and testable.

Mikko
